objectives: Explain why integrating an eye-velocity command requires a persistent neural state after a saccade, and connect bilateral excitation/inhibition to left–right position tuning.
Derive the characteristic equation, eigenvalue-one constraint, and compensating weight family for a general \(2\times 2\) recurrent matrix, while also checking transverse stability.
Use the inverse of a measured F–I curve and fixed synaptic nonlinearities to construct a design matrix, turning an apparently nonlinear circuit fit into row-wise least squares.

prerequisiteBridge: Integration turns velocity into position. If velocity is approximately constant during each short interval \(\Delta t\), the position change is about \(v\Delta t\). Summing many small intervals and taking the continuous limit gives \(x(t)=x(0)+\int v(t')dt'\). After a saccade, the velocity command returns to zero but eye position must not, so a neural circuit has to retain the integrated result. When a linear recurrent mode approaches eigenvalue 1, positive feedback nearly cancels intrinsic leak and creates a long time scale.

A two-by-two matrix W has two eigenvalues. In the rate equation \(\tau dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\), a mode's effective leak is \(1-\lambda\). Perfect linear integration requires at least one task-relevant eigenvalue equal to 1. The other eigenvalue must also lie in the stable range; otherwise the network retains state along the memory direction but explodes in the transverse direction. One functional constraint generally does not determine every synaptic weight uniquely.

Least squares chooses parameters that minimize squared differences between predicted and observed targets. If predictions depend linearly on the weights, the loss surface is a quadratic bowl whose Hessian gives curvature along different parameter directions. Large curvature means a small displacement greatly increases loss and is called stiff; small curvature permits a large displacement with little loss and is called sloppy. These directions live in parameter space, not along neural activity trajectories.

modules.title: Eye-velocity integration, persistent position, and the bilateral circuit
paragraphs: Moving the eye requires phasic motor drive to generate velocity and tonic drive to oppose orbital restoring forces and hold the new position. The course abstracts the distributed brainstem and cerebellar network as a neural integrator: its input is the eye-velocity command \(v(t)\), and its output state approximates \(x(t)=x(0)+\int v(t')dt'\). Ideally, x retains its latest value when v returns to zero; if the network leaks, position slowly drifts back toward center.

The source diagram contains excitatory populations EL and ER and inhibitory populations IL and IR in the left and right hemispheres. Their position-tuning curves have opposite directions: at rightward positions, firing rises in one population and falls in the other. Mutual excitation can prolong the memory mode, while crossed inhibition organizes the left–right push–pull pattern into a signed coordinate. This is a functional architecture; arrows alone do not reveal the strength of each real synapse.

Linear tuning lets a weighted difference of population rates encode eye position. If a right-preferring neuron has \(hR\approx b+kx\) and a left-preferring one \(hL\approx b-kx\), then \(hR-hL\approx 2kx\), while the common baseline \(hR+hL\approx 2b\). The integrator can store signed position in a difference-like mode while keeping the common mode stable. Real neurons have thresholds, saturation, and heterogeneity, so these linear relations hold only over an operating range.

Test the integrator by asking whether firing persists after a velocity pulse, whether the persistent level scales with the pulse integral, and how a network perturbation changes the drift time constant. Position-tuning correlations alone cannot separate sensory eye-position feedback from recurrent memory; comparisons in darkness, feedback perturbations, or circuit interventions are needed.
keyPoints: The time integral of velocity gives position change.
Recurrent positive feedback sustains a persistent state after the command ends.
Opponent tuning in left and right populations can encode signed eye position.
Position-tuning correlations alone do not prove recurrent integration.

derivation.title: From velocity samples to a continuous position integral
derivation.setup: First accumulate position changes in finite time steps, then introduce continuous notation and a leaky neural implementation.

steps.title: Discrete accumulation
steps.explanation: During interval n, position increases by \(v_{n}\Delta t\).

steps.title: Sum all intervals
steps.explanation: The total change from 0 to t is the sum of the increment in each interval.

steps.title: Take the continuous limit
steps.explanation: As \(\Delta t\) shrinks, the Riemann sum approaches an integral.

steps.title: Connect to a neural mode
steps.explanation: Implement leaky integration with \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}} d\alpha /dt=-\alpha +k v\); when \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) is long, the state is approximately retained over a delay.

symbolNotes: Use deg/s for v and deg for x; k maps the units of the velocity command into a neural coordinate.
\(\alpha\) is a population-mode amplitude and need not equal mechanical position.
derivation.unitsCheck: v×dt gives deg, so the integral has the same units as x. In a rate-coordinate neural equation, k must supply any missing units.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\to \infty\) with appropriately scaled input, the system approaches a perfect integrator; with finite \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\), \(\alpha\) drifts exponentially under zero input.

workedExample.title: Accumulate two saccade commands
workedExample.problem: Start at \(x=0 \mathrm{deg}\). Move right at 30 deg/s for 0.08 s, then left at -20 deg/s for 0.05 s. Ignoring leak, find the final position.
steps: The final position is \(x=0+2.4-1.0=+1.4 \mathrm{deg}\), still rightward.
workedExample.result: After the second command ends, an ideal integrator should hold +1.4 deg rather than return to zero.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Signs of velocity must match left–right direction. The total command area \(2.4-1.0=1.4 \mathrm{deg}\) provides a direct check.

pitfalls: Conflating velocity tuning and position tuning as the same population signal.
Treating the bilateral arrows in the schematic as the one measured connectomic implementation.

modules.title: General \(2\times 2\) weights, eigenvalue one, and a compensating family
paragraphs: Let \(W=[[W_{11},W_{12}],[W_{21},W_{22}]]\). Its characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda ^{2}-(W_{11}+W_{22})\lambda +(W_{11}W_{22}-W_{12}W_{21})=0\), and the quadratic formula gives both eigenvalues. For \(\tau dh/dt=-h+Wh\), perfect integration requires an eigenvalue of W equal to 1 because that mode's coefficient \(-(1-\lambda )\) is exactly zero. Substituting \(\lambda =1\) directly is more robust than manipulating the square root and gives \(\det(I-W)=0\).

Expanding gives \(\det(I-W)=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})-W_{12}W_{21}=0\). If \(W_{12}\ne 0\), solve \(W_{21}=(1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})/W_{12}\). Once three weights are chosen, the fourth compensates; increasing a self-weight can be offset by changing cross-coupling while preserving \(\lambda =1\). This is a many-to-one functional mapping: different parameter points share the same integrator eigenvalue.

Do not hide special cases with division. When \(W_{12}=0\), the formula is invalid and the condition becomes \((1-W_{11})(1-W_{22})=0\), so at least one self-weight equals 1. The other eigenvalue must also be checked. Since the sum of the eigenvalues is \(\operatorname{trace}(W)\), if \(\lambda _{1}=1\) then \(\lambda _{2}=W_{11}+W_{22}-1\). Transverse stability of the continuous rate equation requires \(\lambda _{2}<1\). If \(\lambda _{2}\) is also very close to 1, the network acquires another slow mode and may fail to encode position uniquely.

Algebraic satisfaction does not guarantee biological feasibility. Excitatory and inhibitory cell types constrain weight signs, conductance and firing ranges constrain magnitudes, noise makes exact \(\lambda =1\) difficult to maintain, and nonlinear saturation changes large-state dynamics. Study the region of parameter space that gives adequate integration and its robustness, rather than treating a one-parameter relation as a complete circuit solution.
keyPoints: A perfect linear integrator satisfies \(\det(I-W)=0\).
The other eigenvalue must be stable; \(\lambda _{2}=\operatorname{trace}(W)-1\).
Parameter compensation is not measurement noise and does not guarantee biophysical feasibility.

derivation.title: From the characteristic polynomial to an integrator family
derivation.setup: Keep the matrix general rather than assuming symmetry, and handle the boundary case for division separately.

steps.title: Write the characteristic polynomial
steps.explanation: The two-by-two determinant produces the trace–determinant form.

steps.title: Set the memory eigenvalue to 1
steps.explanation: Substitute \(\lambda =1\) and rearrange.

steps.title: Solve the compensating relation
steps.explanation: Isolate W21 only when W12 is nonzero.

steps.title: Check the transverse root
steps.explanation: Because the roots sum to the trace, the other root is the trace minus 1.

symbolNotes: Wij are dimensionless effective recurrent gains.
Eigenvalue 1 belongs to W; the corresponding root of the full generator is \((\lambda -1)/\tau\).
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\det(I-W)\) is dimensionless. \(\tau\) appears only when converting an eigenvalue gap into a time constant.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(W_{12}\to 0\), the family formula becomes numerically unbounded, signaling that one should return to the undivided constraint rather than infer an infinite synapse.

workedExample.title: Solve for the fourth weight and check stability
workedExample.problem: Let \(W_{11}=0.8\), \(W_{22}=0.7\), and \(W_{12}=0.2\). Find W21 so that one mode is a perfect integrator, then check the other mode.
steps: Its full transverse coefficient is \(-(1-0.5)/\tau =-0.5/\tau\), so that mode decays stably.
workedExample.result: \(W=[[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]]\) has eigenvalues 1 and 0.5, giving one memory mode and one stable transverse mode.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The \(\operatorname{trace} 1.5\) equals 1+0.5, and the determinant 0.5 equals \(1\times 0.5\), providing two checks.

pitfalls: Replacing the general matrix with the symmetric two-neuron special case and missing asymmetric compensation.
Checking \(\det(I-W)=0\) without checking \(\lambda _{2}\), input projection, and readout.

modules.title: Biological variability and reparameterizing a nonlinear circuit fit
paragraphs: Following work by Goldman, Marder, and others, this lesson emphasizes that different parameter settings can produce similar voltage or behavioral dynamics; variability across animals need not destroy function. Approximately linear position tuning in the oculomotor integrator lets researchers measure rates at several eye positions and ask which sets of synaptic weights reproduce those states. This variability concerns model or individual parameters, not recording noise.

For postsynaptic neuron i, measure the target rate \(h_{i}(p\mu )\) at position \(p\mu\) and use the measured inverse F–I curve to convert it into the required net current \(Y_{i}\mu =F_{i}^{-1}(h_{i}(p\mu ))\). For each presynaptic neuron j, pass its rate through a fixed synaptic nonlinearity \(S_{E}\) or \(S_{I}\) to obtain feature \(X_{j}\mu\). Add a row of constant 1 values for bias current. The complicated biophysics is thereby precomputed into Y and X.

With the nonlinear functions fixed, the prediction is \(\hat{Y}_{i\mu }=\sum _j W_{ij} X_{j}\mu\), linear in the unknown weights Wij and bias. Each output neuron i can fit one row of weights independently. If M sample positions are columns, X has shape D×M, Y is N×M, W is N×D, and \(\hat{Y}=WX\) is dimensionally consistent. State this orientation explicitly, because placing samples in rows yields a transposed formula.

The boundary of this reparameterization matters. If the inverse F–I estimate is wrong, the synaptic threshold is fitted jointly, features are highly correlated, or noise is heteroscedastic, simple OLS gives unreliable uncertainty. Different nonlinear assumptions can yield different weight ensembles that fit the rates equally well. 'Linearized fitting' is a conditional computational convenience, not a claim that the native circuit lacks nonlinearities.
keyPoints: First use \(F_{i}^{-1}\) to convert each target rate into required current.
Once synaptic nonlinearities are fixed, their outputs become design-matrix features.
With samples as columns, \(Y=N\times M\), \(X=D\times M\), and \(W=N\times D\).
Linear in the weights does not mean that the entire biological model is linear.

derivation.title: From a steady-state circuit equation to \(Y=WX\)
derivation.setup: At every measured position, evaluate the known nonlinear terms first and leave only the weights unknown.

steps.title: Construct target current
steps.explanation: For every output i and sample \(\mu\), evaluate the inverse F–I curve.

steps.title: Construct the features
steps.explanation: Pass every presynaptic rate through its E or I synaptic function, then append a constant bias feature.

steps.title: Write the linear prediction
steps.explanation: The weights appear only as coefficients of the features.

steps.title: Stack into matrices
steps.explanation: Arrange all outputs and positions simultaneously.

symbolNotes: M is the number of positions/samples, D is the number of features including bias, and N is the number of output neurons.
Signs for E and I can be placed in constraints on W or in feature definitions, but the convention must remain consistent.
derivation.unitsCheck: \((N\times D)(D\times M)=N\times M\), matching Y; every column corresponds to the same eye position.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(F_{i}\) is not invertible or the rate lies on a saturation plateau, \(F_{i}^{-1}\) is not unique and target-current construction fails.

workedExample.title: Build one design row and predict current
workedExample.problem: At two positions, an output has features \(x_{1}=[1,2]\) and \(x_{2}=[3,1]\), with an additional bias 1 at both. The weights are \([w_{1},w_{2},b]=[0.5,-1,2]\). Find both predictions.
steps: At position 1, the feature vector is (1,2,1) and the prediction is \(0.5\times 1-1\times 2+2=0.5\).
At position 2, the feature vector is (3,1,1) and the prediction is \(0.5\times 3-1\times 1+2=2.5\).
workedExample.result: The target-current predictions at the two positions are 0.5 and 2.5; matrix and term-by-term calculations agree.
workedExample.sanityCheck: W has shape \(1\times 3\) and X has shape \(3\times 2\), so the output must be \(1\times 2\). An answer of \(2\times 1\) indicates that sample orientation was reversed.

pitfalls: Treating parameter variability and observation noise as the same source.
Applying \(YX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\) without stating sample orientation and obtaining incompatible shapes.

modules.title: Least squares, the closed-form solution, and the Hessian
paragraphs: With samples as columns, write the loss \(L(W)=1/2||Y-WX||_F^{2}\). The Frobenius norm sums squared residuals across all outputs and samples. Output rows are independent, so begin with one weight row w and target row y: \(L(w)=1/2(y-wX)(y-wX)^\mathrm{T}\). Expanding gives the constant \(yy^\mathrm{T}\), the linear term \(-yX^\mathrm{T}w^\mathrm{T}\), and the quadratic term wXX^\(Tw^\mathrm{T}\).

Differentiating with respect to w gives gradient \((wX-y)X^\mathrm{T}\). Setting it to zero gives the normal equation wXX^\(T=yX^\mathrm{T}\). If \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is invertible, \(\hat{w}=yX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\); stacking all rows gives \(\hat{W}=YX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\). If features are collinear, \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is singular and requires a pseudoinverse, regularization, or redesigned samples.

Near the optimum, let \(\Delta w=w-\hat{w}\). The normal equation eliminates the cross term, leaving \(L=L\min+1/2 \Delta w H \Delta w^\mathrm{T}\) with \(H=XX^\mathrm{T}\). The same feature Hessian applies row by row to the full W, or appears in blocks after vectorizing the parameters. H depends only on design features for this local curvature; changing the noise model or constraints changes the effective Hessian.

This connects fitting with experimental design. If one feature combination barely changes across positions, X contains little information along that direction and H has a small eigenvalue. Conditions that selectively activate that combination can increase curvature and tighten parameter uncertainty. Sloppiness need not be accepted passively; perturbations and improved sampling can reduce it.
keyPoints: The OLS loss is \(1/2||Y-WX||^{2}\).
When the inverse exists, \(\hat{W}=YX^\mathrm{T}(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\).
\(H=XX^\mathrm{T}\) describes parameter curvature supported by the features.
Collinear features make H singular or nearly singular, requiring regularization or new experiments.

derivation.title: From quadratic loss to the OLS closed form
derivation.setup: Derive one output row first; multiple outputs simply repeat the calculation side by side.

steps.title: Write the loss
steps.explanation: The residual row is y-wX.

steps.title: Compute the gradient
steps.explanation: Differentiate with respect to each weight and collect the results as a row vector.

steps.title: Solve the normal equation
steps.explanation: Set the gradient to zero, then right-multiply by the inverse.

steps.title: Identify the Hessian
steps.explanation: Differentiate the gradient once more with respect to w.

symbolNotes: w is 1×D, X is D×M, y is 1×M, and H is D×D.
For multiple outputs, W is N×D and the formula applies to every row simultaneously.
derivation.unitsCheck: \((1\times D)(D\times M)=1\times M\), and \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is D×D. Every term in the loss has squared target-current units.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(M<D\) or the features are linearly dependent, \(\operatorname{rank}(XX^\mathrm{T})<D\) and the ordinary inverse does not exist. A pseudoinverse selects a minimum-norm solution but does not remove the identifiability problem.

workedExample.title: Identifiability from a two-feature Hessian
workedExample.problem: Let \(X=[[1,0,1],[0,1,1]]\). Compute \(H=XX^\mathrm{T}\) and determine whether it is invertible.
steps: \(\det(H)=4-1=3>0\), so H is invertible; its eigenvalues are 3 and 1.
workedExample.result: Both parameter combinations are identifiable, but curvature along the common-feature direction is 3 and exceeds the difference-direction curvature of 1.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The \(\operatorname{trace} 4\) must equal the eigenvalue \(\operatorname{sum} 3+1\), and the determinant 3 must equal the product \(3\times 1\).

pitfalls: Treating existence of a closed-form inverse as proof that the biological parameters are unique.
Ignoring feature scaling; different units directly alter Hessian eigenvalues and comparisons of stiffness.

modules.title: The Hessian eigenbasis, stiff/sloppy directions, and model ensembles
paragraphs: A Hessian is symmetric positive-semidefinite, so \(H=VDV^\mathrm{T}\), where columns \(v_{k}\) are orthonormal parameter directions and D contains \(\lambda _{k}\ge 0\). Let \(z=V^\mathrm{T}(w-\hat{w})\); then the quadratic loss increase is \(\Delta L=1/2\sum \lambda _{k} z_{k}^{2}\). A large \(\lambda _{k}\) gives a large loss for the same displacement and defines a stiff direction. A small \(\lambda _{k}\) permits farther movement within the adequate-fit contour and defines a sloppy direction.

The fit shown on this lesson has about 4 stiff and 46 sloppy dimensions. Those counts belong to that model, dataset, and parameterization; they are not universal constants of oculomotor circuits. In a two-direction example, the error contour is an elongated ellipse: its short axis corresponds to large \(\lambda\) and its long axis to small \(\lambda\). Each axis is generally a mixture of many weights, so calling one parameter sloppy is often imprecise.

Sloppiness can reflect genuine functional compensation, but also failure of an experiment to excite certain modes, large measurement noise, collinear features, or poor parameter scaling. It does not make the associated biology irrelevant. A direction that is sloppy for the current eye-position dataset may matter during perturbation, development, or another behavior. New conditions are needed to distinguish biological degeneracy from insufficient data.

Reporting one best-fit W hides this structure. Instead, collect all models with loss below a prespecified adequacy threshold, compare their common predictions, and identify experiments on which they disagree most. A perturbation outcome predicted by every model is robust; divergence along a sloppy valley identifies an experiment that can narrow the ensemble. Sloppiness in parameter space is distinct from low dimensionality of neural states in Lecture19.
keyPoints: \(\Delta L=1/2\sum \lambda _{k} z_{k}^{2}\) decomposes curvature along parameter eigen-directions.
Large \(\lambda\) is stiff; small \(\lambda\) is sloppy.
A sloppy direction usually combines multiple parameters and does not mean that one synapse is irrelevant.
An adequate-model ensemble expresses uncertainty and robust predictions better than a single best fit.

derivation.title: Derive ellipse-axis lengths from curvature
derivation.setup: In a two-dimensional Hessian eigenbasis, fix the allowable loss increase and find how far one may move along each direction.

steps.title: Diagonalize H
steps.explanation: Use \(z=V^\mathrm{T}\Delta w\) to eliminate cross terms.

steps.title: Set the adequacy threshold
steps.explanation: Let \(\Delta L\le c\); the boundary is \(\sum \lambda _{k} z_{k}^{2}=2c\).

steps.title: Find an axis radius
steps.explanation: Along axis k, set all other coordinates to 0.

steps.title: Compare stiff and sloppy
steps.explanation: Radius is proportional to \(1/\sqrt \lambda\); an eigenvalue ratio of 10000 gives an axis-length ratio of 100.

symbolNotes: \(z_{k}\) uses parameter units after rotation by V; if the original parameters have different units, scale them sensibly first.
c is the permitted loss increase; its statistical interpretation depends on the noise model.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\lambda _{k}\) has units of loss/\(parameter^{2}\), so taking the square root of \(2c/\lambda _{k}\) restores parameter units.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(\lambda _{k}=0\), the quadratic approximation gives an infinitely flat direction, meaning that the data do not constrain that combination at all. Actual bounds or higher-order terms may truncate it.

workedExample.title: Compare two curvature directions
workedExample.problem: The Hessian eigenvalues are 100 and 0.01, and the allowed \(\Delta L\) is 0.5. Find the maximum displacement along each axis and their ratio.
steps: The ratio is \(10/0.1=100\); at the same loss tolerance, the sloppy direction permits a displacement 100 times larger.
workedExample.result: The adequate-fit ellipse is extremely long along the small-eigenvalue direction, directly visualizing parameter compensation or weak constraint.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The eigenvalue ratio is \(100/0.01=10000\), so the axis ratio is its square root, 100, not 10000.

pitfalls: Comparing Hessian eigenvalues of unstandardized parameters and creating artificial sloppiness through unit differences.
Interchanging parameter-space Hessian eigenvectors with neural-activity PCs or dynamical modes.

figures.title: Three fates of an eigenvalue-one integrator
figures.alt: After the command ends, a mode whose eigenvalue is less than one decays, a mode equal to one persists, and a mode greater than one grows.
figures.caption: After input is removed, the fate of the same initial mode amplitude depends only on \(1-\lambda\): when \(\lambda <1\) it leaks; when \(\lambda =1\) the restoring coefficient in the derivative vanishes and memory persists; when \(\lambda >1 a\) small deviation grows. Thus \(\det(I-W)=0\) guarantees only an integrating mode, and the stability of all remaining modes must still be checked.
